books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Wilmot Proviso, amendment offered by David Wilmot (D-PA) to an appropriations bill, August 8, 1846. Public domain.
stimulus.text: Provided, That, as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico by the United States, by virtue of any treaty which may be negotiated between them, and to the use by the Executive of the moneys herein appropriated, neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist in any part of said territory, except for crime, whereof the party shall first be duly convicted.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Wilmot Proviso, August 8, 1846, public domain
stem: The Proviso is best understood as an attempt to

options.text: admit California as a slave state.
options.misconception: The Proviso would ban slavery in land from Mexico, which includes California; it would not admit California as a slave state.

options.text: prevent slavery from spreading into land taken from Mexico.
end slavery in the states where it already existed.
options.misconception: The Proviso applied only to territory acquired from Mexico, not to slavery in the existing states.

options.text: give the president power to decide where slavery would be allowed.
options.misconception: The Proviso would fix the rule by law — no slavery in the new territory — not leave it to the president.

rationales.A: The Proviso would ban slavery in territory from Mexico, including California; it points the other way from admitting a slave state.
rationales.B: The Proviso says that in any territory acquired from Mexico “neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist” — a ban on slavery's spread into the new land.
rationales.C: The Proviso covers only territory to be acquired from Mexico; it says nothing about slavery in the states where it already existed.
rationales.D: The Proviso sets the rule itself by law; it does not hand the decision to the president.
rationales.general:
1. Find what the Proviso covers. It covers “any territory” acquired from Mexico by treaty.
2. Find what it orders. In that territory, “neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist.”
3. Name the move. It does not free anyone already enslaved; it draws a line against slavery spreading into new land.
Remember: a ban on spreading is not a ban on existing. The Proviso's fight was about the future of the West, not the present of the South.
